General.Description:
The village of Ututu has stood at the bend of the same river for six hundred years. Its people know the river's moods — the dry-season shallows, the flood-season fury, the particular quality of light on the water in the hour before a storm. They have built their economy, their calendar, their cosmology around the river. When the oil company arrives with extraction permits and environmental assessments that describe the river as a resource rather than a relation, the village does not know, at first, how to respond.

When Rivers Speak tells the story of four generations of one family in Ututu across a hundred and twenty years — from the colonial era to the environmental crisis of the present day. James Okafor moves with equal authority across all four timelines, weaving voices and registers with a structural confidence that is remarkable for a debut novelist.

What the novel ultimately asks — and refuses to answer too simply — is what community means in the face of forces larger than community, and what is lost when the world that formed a people's self-understanding is physically destroyed.

Okafor writes with compassion, precision, and a controlled fury that gives every page moral weight. One of the finest debut novels of the year.
